t: Count Unhappy Friends - Rank Tables Turn Preference Tests Into O(1)
o:
## Understanding the problem

Everyone is paired up. Person x is unhappy if there exists some other person u such that x ranks u above x's own partner AND u ranks x above u's own partner. Both conditions must hold simultaneously for the same witness u; a single disappointed preference is not enough.

In example 1, friend 1 is paired with 0 but ranks 3 first, and friend 3 (paired with 2) ranks 1 first - so 1 is unhappy, and the same mutual preference makes 3 unhappy too, for an answer of 2. Friends 0 and 2 find nobody who prefers them over their partners, so they stay happy.

With n up to 500 there are about 250000 (x, u) pairs to test, so O(n^2) checks after O(1) preference comparisons is the target; naive list searches hidden inside the loop would silently push the runtime toward O(n^3).
k: Precompute rank[x][u] = position of u in x's preference list so every prefers-test becomes one array read.
x is unhappy exactly when some u satisfies rank[x][u] < rank[x][partner[x]] and rank[u][x] < rank[u][partner[u]].
Scanning x's preference list in order allows an early break: anyone ranked at or below the partner can never serve as a witness.

a.n: Approach 1: Direct Simulation With Linear Searches
a.i: Translate the definition verbatim: for each person x and each candidate u, locate both preference positions with a linear search and evaluate the two inequalities. There is no preprocessing and little room for bugs, but each comparison conceals an O(n) search, adding an unwanted factor of n.
s: Record every person's partner from the pairs list.
For each x, loop over all u different from x and from x's partner.
Find u and both partners inside the relevant preference lists by linear search.
If both inequalities hold, count x as unhappy and stop early.
a.t: O(n^3) - O(n^2) candidate pairs, each costing O(n) in linear searches.

a.n: Approach 2: Rank Tables With Early Exit
a.i: Flatten every preference list into rank[x][u] up front, turning each comparison into an array read. For each x, walk its own preference list from most to least preferred; once we reach someone ranked at or below the partner, no later candidate can qualify, so we break. The first qualifying witness proves unhappiness immediately. Overall quadratic time with tiny constants - comfortably within limits.
s: Build the n by n rank table from the preference lists.
Fill the partner array from the pairs list.
For each x, iterate u over preferences[x] in order.
Break as soon as rank[x][u] >= rank[x][partner[x]].
Otherwise check rank[u][x] < rank[u][partner[u]]; on success count x and break.
a.t: O(n^2) - building the rank table dominates; per-person scans amortize to linear.

w: Always build the rank table first; interviewers specifically watch for the O(n^3) trap hidden inside index-style lookups. Pitfalls: demanding several witnesses at once (a single qualifying u suffices), forgetting that u ranges over everyone except x and x's partner, and double-counting since unhappiness is a property of one person at a time even when it arises from a mutual pair. Edge cases: perfectly stable configurations returning 0, and mutual dissatisfaction like example 1 correctly counting both members. Likely follow-ups: minimum swaps to make everyone happy, or listing all unstable pairs - which this loop already visits.
